newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU agrees BSE aid package despite German qualms.
newsitem.headline: EU agrees BSE aid package despite German qualms.

text.p: European Union farm ministers agreed in the face of German opposition on Wednesday to give an extra 500 million Ecus in aid to farmers hurt by the mad cow crisis and to cut beef surpluses, EU officials said.

France, Germany and Britain are to get over half the aid, which supplements 850 million Ecus agreed by EU leaders in Florence in June. It is to be financed from savings within the bloc's agricultural budget.
"It was agreed by a majority vote with only Germany against," an EU official told reporters after a three-day marathon meeting.

Another official said Germany voted against the package because it believed certain measures were contrary to long term reforms needed to bring the market back into balance and were unfavourable for German farmers.

It rejected a planned single aid payment to bull breeders as too low for grass-fed herds in northern Germany. It also wanted a specific target for reducing suckler cow quotas and a better balance between traditional and intensive farming.
Britain welcomed the agreement, noting British farmers will get 50 million pounds, or 13.1 percent of the total aid. This is just over one percent more than originally proposed.
"We came here to fight for U.K. farmers. This further substantial aid package should be very welcome to them," British Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg said in a statement.
France and Germany will receive the lion's share of the extra aid, with 23.8 percent and 20 percent respectively.

Measures to cut beef surpluses include the removal of at least one million calves through the offer of a so-called "Herod premium" to slaughter new-born male calves or an incentive scheme to market young lightweight cattle.
The crisis was triggered by a British government statement in March that the fatal cattle brain disease, bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), could be transmitted to people.
EU beef demand has since fallen 15 percent and some 400,000 tonnes of unwanted beef has been taken into public stores. Farmers' losses are estimated at 1.2 billion Ecus in 1996.
